segments.caption: XGBoost, SVM, KNN, logistic regression. The interviewer asks: which one would you use, and why?
Most people guess. After this video, you won't. Save it!
Choosing an algorithm comes down to 3 questions.
1: do you have the answers, the labels? 2: are you predicting a number, or a category? 3: is it images, audio or text?
Predicting a number? Start with linear regression.
It draws the line that best fits your data. Bigger flat, higher rent.
Need more accuracy on table data? Gradient boosting, like XGBoost.
Trees are built one after another, and each new tree fixes the mistakes of the last one. It wins most competitions on table data.
Predicting a category, like yes or no? Start with logistic regression.
It squeezes everything into a probability between 0 and 1. Will this customer buy? 80%, yes.
Need to explain every decision? A decision tree.
A flowchart of yes or no questions. Salary above 50,000? Any existing loans? Approve, or reject.
Want a stronger, safer choice? Random forest.
Build hundreds of trees, each on a different slice of the data, and let them vote. Banks use it to catch fraud.
Classifying text, like spam? Naive Bayes.
It counts how often words appear in spam versus normal mail. Free, winner, urgent? Probably spam.
Small dataset, two clear classes? A support vector machine.
It draws the widest possible street between the classes. The points on the edge are the support vectors.
The simplest idea of all? K nearest neighbours.
To label a new point, look at its closest neighbours, and copy the majority.
No labels at all, and you want groups? K means clustering.
It drops K centres, gives each point to the nearest one, and moves the centres until the groups settle. Perfect for customer segments.
Too many columns? PCA.
It squeezes 100 columns into a few that keep most of the information. Faster models, easier plots.
Images, audio or text at scale? Neural networks.
Layers of tiny calculators passing signals forward. Stack enough, and you get deep learning: face unlock, ChatGPT.
Learning by trial and reward, like a game? Reinforcement learning.
An agent tries moves, gets rewards or penalties, and learns the best strategy. That's how AI mastered chess.

scenes.title: What to say in the interview

segments.caption: So in the interview, say this. A number? Linear regression, then boosting. A category? Logistic regression, then random forest. Text? Naive Bayes. No labels? K means. Too many columns? PCA. Images? Neural networks.
